notes: Source titles marked titleVerified:false were taken from URL slugs or dossier labels because the ledger has no exact titles. The fact-checker should confirm them against the live pages.
Sentences marked ledger:null are uncited editorial statements based on the dossier (absence of evidence, definitions).

claims.sentence: Meta paused conversation sharing in its Muse AI agent on Oct 20, 2026, after security firm Claroc said one passive-DNS search turned up more than 6,800 Muse share addresses, some holding loan applications and private business documents.

A SenseNova-led preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, reports that OpenAI's GPT-6-Astra scored 81.9% on the RoboDojo robot benchmark with up to 10 times the usual step budget, but 27.6% at the standard budget, below the paper's listed prior best of 29.6% (31.4% for the best prior agentic method).
claims.note: Rewrite per factcheck.json: 31.4% (PhysicalRSI) is in the r8 ledger quote of Table 2.

claims.sentence: Sphinx, a free MIT-licensed Git hook whose Show HN post drew 252 points and 89 comments, quizzes developers on their AI agent's code before a push goes through, though its authors call it 'practice, not a security gate.'
Meta has paused conversation sharing in Muse, its personal AI agent, after Ars Technica asked about research showing that strangers could find shared chats.
The security firm Claroc says a single search of passive-DNS records, databases that log the web addresses devices look up, returned more than 6,800 Muse share addresses.
Meta has not published a statement of its own. Its only comment came by email, to Ars Technica and to The Verge.
claims.note: No-published-post claim rests on dossier search of about.fb.com on 2026-10-21 (Unverified / gaps).

claims.sentence: Sep 8, 2026. Meta launches Muse, calling it "a secure, private personal AI agent".
Meta says it can "open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on their behalf".
Sep 21. Ars Technica reports a zero-day, a flaw unknown to the maker, found by Patrick Wardle. It let local apps take over a Muse account, and Meta later said it shipped a hotfix.
claims.note: Sep 21 is the Ars article date.

claims.sentence: Oct 8. Claroc reports the problem to Meta's bug bounty program "with reproduction steps and example shares".
Asaf Aprozper, Claroc's co-founder and CTO, told Ars he got no reply through the program or on LinkedIn.
Oct 18. Claroc publishes its write-up and names the issue "GhostShares": pages "that open for people who were never handed the link".
"If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort. It took one query," the team writes.
Oct 20. Ars Technica's Dan Goodin reports the findings. In response to Ars's questions, Meta says it is pausing sharing.
Muse spokesperson Tracy Clayton sends The Verge the same statement.
Claroc updates its post: 40 shares it rechecked no longer opened.
Muse built each share's web address from the conversation's title plus a random ID.
Opening a share makes the browser look up that address, and DNS logs the whole name, "random ID and all".
The part meant to be unguessable got recorded with everything else.
Every share used the domain cf.metaaiusercontent.com.
Ars traces the problem to "putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path".
Muse's robots.txt file keeps search crawlers out, but "robots.txt governs crawling, not access," Claroc notes.
The public scanning service urlscan.io also held more than 75 saved scans of share pages, Claroc says.
Claroc opened only a few hundred pages and says most were "unremarkable," such as small-business sites and event calendars.

A minority were sensitive. Opened with no login, they included a home-sale budget, a small-business loan application, a revenue review meant only for a CEO and a job candidate's confidential notes for a call with an AI lab.
Claroc says it has no evidence anyone misused the shares.
Claroc sells a browser extension that flags public AI share links, so it has a commercial interest in the finding.
We found no independent report reproducing its 6,800 count, and Claroc says its study "is not a measure of Muse's total exposure".
claims.note: First clause rests on dossier section 5 and Unverified / gaps.

claims.sentence: Meta's statement treats the pages as working as built: a share "creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link".
In 2025, OpenAI removed an option that let shared ChatGPT chats be indexed by search engines.
More than 370,000 shared Grok chats turned up in search results.
Muse is widely used, with 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, per Sensor Tower data reported by TechCrunch.
claims.note: Background only; no country framing in body. Source title names a country and is exempt per style guide.

claims.sentence: Meta told Ars it will "review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered". It gave no timeline.
The pause does not erase the record: the hostnames, "titles included, are still in passive-DNS history," Claroc reports.
OpenAI's GPT-6-Astra, a general-purpose AI model, scored 81.9% on the RoboDojo robot benchmark, but only with up to 10 times the usual step budget, a SenseNova-led team reports.
claims.note: 'SenseNova-led' per dossier section 3 / r37; no institutions named. Round 1: entry corrected to match the draft text (previous entry held an older lead sentence).

claims.sentence: At the standard budget it scored 27.6%.
claims.note: Round 1: entry added; sentence was in the draft but missing from the map.

claims.sentence: The authors are upfront about the catch: the best results come only when the model studies demonstrations first and gets many more moves than usual.
The report was posted to arXiv on Oct 15 and revised Oct 19. It is a preprint, not yet peer-reviewed.
The team's verdict is that Astra "has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence".
"Embodied" here means controlling a physical body, such as a robot arm.
OpenAI is not an author, and it pitched Astra in September for computer use, coding, cybersecurity and science, not robotics.
The team ran Astra on 12 benchmarks covering tabletop arms, humanoids, mobile robots and dexterous hands.

First, in-context learning: Astra reads each benchmark's training demonstrations and writes a frozen "knowledge package" of notes and reusable code, while its weights, the model's learned settings, stay unchanged.
Second, an extended budget that "allows ten times as many action steps as the standard budget".
Table row 1: 81.9% on RoboDojo, far above the paper's listed prior best of 29.6% (31.4% for the best prior agentic method); at the standard cutoff in the same run, Astra scored 27.6%, below both.
claims.note: Rewrite per factcheck.json: 31.4% (PhysicalRSI) is in the r8 ledger quote of Table 2.

claims.sentence: Table row 2: 61.5% on Bench2Dex only with extended budget; ties pi0.5 at standard budget, 25.6% to 25.5%.
Table row 3: SIMPLE 70.8% to 90.8% at standard budget; Zhang et al. no aggregate benefit; RoboICL reports gains with interaction memory.
Table row 4: 8 platforms, no demonstrations; pick-and-place 17/18, cloth folding 2/4, navigation and search 9/23, plug insertion 0/11.
The authors concede that Astra's benchmark results "depend heavily on conditions that the benchmarks grant".
Simulators pause while the model thinks. On RoboDojo, the standard budgets equal 8 to 76 seconds of robot motion, against an average of 55 minutes of computing.
Under the extended budget, one RoboDojo episode averages more than three hours.
The team also built a prototype household test where the clock keeps running. Astra took 8 seconds of world time to decide to turn off a burner, and the egg charred.
It also left a refrigerator door open from 300 to 765 seconds.
On the Unitree G1 humanoid, Astra spent about 90% of each run deliberating, and one manipulation trial took over an hour.
On one robot hand it completed 0 of 3 grasps without human-written grasp routines and 3 of 3 with them.
One LIBERO-Long++ episode used about a million tokens, the chunks of text a model processes, and nearly an hour.
The authors estimate roughly $1 per million tokens, since about 98% are cached input.
The independent leaderboard Artificial Analysis ranks Astra first on its AA-Robotics v0.1 test with a score of 69, at an average of 30 minutes and $16.36 per task.
It finds today's models "roughly 100 times slower than a human".

One outside warning comes from Zhang et al., another preprint not yet peer-reviewed: "Testing was halted after the model repeatedly issued physically unreasonable or unsafe actions, including incidents that damaged hardware; no person was injured".
claims.note: Quote is in the PDF full text (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.24170).

claims.sentence: Robocurve's RoboHarm test reports that Astra refused 2 of 100 harmful robot-arm instructions on safety grounds (3 of 100 counting refusals for any reason).
claims.note: Rewrite per factcheck.json: the safety-vs-any-reason split (2 vs 3 of 100) comes from the fact-checker's reading of the RoboHarm page; the r34 ledger entry still carries the outdated 'appears to sum to 3' note and should be corrected.

claims.sentence: The robotics company Pantograph saw runs end with the model "confidently claiming that the towel is in the hamper, when it is clearly visible on the floor".
Sphinx is a free, MIT-licensed Git hook, a script Git runs automatically before an action such as a push, and it asks you a question about what your AI agent's code does before it ships.
claims.note: Round 1 rewrite: the Git hook definition clause is an editorial definition (ledger:null for that clause), added per editor advisory.

claims.sentence: Its npm package was first published Oct 16 and is at version 0.1.11.
The Show HN post on Oct 18 drew 252 points and 89 comments.
When you push to a protected branch, Git waits while Sphinx asks you to predict what your change will do. Miss something and it explains, then offers a new scenario. Pass and the push continues.
A separate reviewer model writes the questions. It reads the change with read-only Git tools and never sees the conversation that produced the code.
Questions cover "behavior, failure modes, and invariants rather than file names or function names," and the check is open-book.
It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Pi or plain Git, and "your answers never reach the coding agent".
The reviewer runs on your own Claude Code or Codex plan, OpenRouter or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
A typical check makes about 5 to 8 model requests, with no default cap.
"This is practice, not a security gate. Anyone with local access, including a coding agent, can bypass hooks or get outside help".
One commenter wrote, "Nothing prevents a lazy person from copy-pasting the question to the agent".
claims.note: Capitalization restored to match the original comment.

claims.sentence: A commenter separated "understanding what a PR does versus knowing how to tell if it's wrong".
The authors' own tests used "five small, synthetic Git repositories" and were "not an all-green semantic evaluation".
In one case the grader rejected a correct answer, and a second model, Sonnet 5.5, "reproduced the material false negative".
claims.note: Round 1 rewrite: 'stronger' changed to 'second'; the source names the model but does not rank it.

claims.sentence: Your changed code also goes to the reviewer provider, and version 0.1 checks only local commits and pushes.
Commenters pointed to similar tools, including PEAK, built about six months earlier.
One liked that it "tests whether the person understands the change instead of adding another AI reviewer".
The landing page jokingly credits its epigraph to "Sun Tzu." The line, "you can outsource your thinking / but you cannot outsource your understanding," comes from an X post by @yacineMTB.
